snippet.title: She's Been Waiting 3 Years for Her Passion to Find Her (Narrated Live)
snippet.description:
Three years ago, Cella heard "find your passion, and you'll never work a day in your life." She's been waiting for it ever since. Fourteen hobbies, all quit in week two. Two commentators call it live.

For the friend who's been "finding their passion" since 2023.

Chapters
0:00 Day 1,096
0:45 The record
1:29 The sign
2:07 Week two, live
2:32 Halftime: found, or built?
4:15 Replay: the coach's side
5:01 Also tonight: your closet
5:23 Week three
6:03 Full time

The idea at halftime comes from five studies by psychologists Paul O'Keefe, Carol Dweck and Gregory Walton, published in 2018. College students who believed passions are found, not built, were more likely to expect that a passion brings endless motivation. In another study, community college students watched an engaging video about black holes and then read a difficult scientific article on it; those who had just read that passions are found lost more of their interest than those who read that passions are built. These were short studies of interest in a topic, measured over minutes; careers over years were not measured.
O'Keefe, P. A., Dweck, C. S., & Walton, G. M. (2018). Implicit theories of interest: Finding your passion or developing it? Psychological Science, 29(10), 1653-1664. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797618780643

The passion coach is a made-up character. Any resemblance to a real coach is the genre's fault.

snippet.title: Self-Help Tier List: Ranked by Actual Evidence
snippet.description:
For the friend who sent you a "manifest it" post this week.

We took twelve famous pieces of self-help advice and ranked them S to F by what the studies found. One of them made people more aggressive than doing nothing. Four have no data at all. And one tier stays empty.

The tiers: S, works, and big. A, solid. B, small but real. C, something's there, and the poster oversells it. D, didn't hold up. F, worse than doing nothing. NO DATA, we found no study that tested it as advice. The ranking is ours; the studies are below, with their limits.

Which poster is on your wall? Tell us, we'll rank it.

Chapters
0:00 The board
0:32 The rules (and Cella wants S)
1:11 Vent it out
2:28 Say "I am a lovable person"
3:33 Power pose
4:21 Speed round: no data
5:11 Manifest it
6:37 Willpower battery and 10,000 hours
7:46 Write about what hurts, and say thank you
9:32 The empty row

The studies:
Bushman (2002): 600 students were insulted, then hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who insulted them, or while thinking about getting fit, or sat still for two minutes. The "venting" group was the angriest and the most aggressive afterwards; sitting still was the least. One lab study with students.
Wood, Perunovic & Lee (2009): in a lab study with 68 students, people with low self-esteem who repeated "I am a lovable person" felt worse than those who didn't; people with high self-esteem felt somewhat better. Small groups, one session.
Ranehill et al. (2015): about 200 people in Zurich held power poses or not. No difference in testosterone, cortisol or risk taking; the posers reported feeling more powerful.
Oettingen & Mayer (2002): in four correlational studies (40 job seekers followed for two years, students with a crush, students before an exam, hip-surgery patients), more positive fantasies went with worse outcomes; positive expectations went with better ones. Kappes & Oettingen (2011): in four small experiments with students, positive fantasies lowered energy (self-report and systolic blood pressure); in one, students reported getting less done the following week.
Hagger et al. (2016): 23 labs, 2,141 people, the same preregistered "willpower depletion" task (one version of the task). The effect was close to zero (d = 0.04).
Macnamara, Hambrick & Oswald (2014): 88 studies. Deliberate practice explained about 12% of the differences in performance; about 26% in games, 21% in music, 18% in sports, 4% in education, under 1% in professions.
The "3% of Yale graduates who wrote down their goals" study: Yale University Library says no such study occurred; no record was found, and the class secretary and the classmates he asked didn't know of it (ask.library.yale.edu/faq/175224).
Pennebaker & Beall (1986): 46 students in four groups (trivial topics; a trauma, facts only; feelings only; or both) wrote for 15 minutes a day, four days in a row. In the following months, the 11 who wrote about a trauma with both facts and feelings did not increase their visits to the student health center; the other groups went about once more each (p = .055, marginal).
Frattaroli (2006): a meta-analysis of 146 randomized studies (about 11,000 people) on writing or talking about feelings. A small effect (r = .075).
Emmons & McCullough (2003, Study 1): students who listed five things they were grateful for, weekly for ten weeks, felt better about their life as a whole and more optimistic about the coming week than students who listed hassles, and reported about 1.3 more hours of exercise a week than the hassles group. Self-reported; not every result repeated in Studies 2 and 3.
"Live, laugh, love", "protect your peace", "everything happens for a reason": we didn't find a study that tested them as advice.

snippet.title: The Church of the Holy Hustle
snippet.description:
For the friend who sends emails at 5 a.m. and then posts about it.

Welcome to Sunday service at the Church of the Holy Hustle: a hymn at 5 a.m. and a baptism in cold brew. Then the newcomer, Cella, asks a question nobody asks here: does the seventieth hour of work actually do anything? An analyst in the last pew has the answer, from a British munitions factory in 1916. Cella gets excommunicated. On Monday at 5 a.m., she's back in the pew.

What time is your alarm set for tomorrow? And who is it for?

Chapters
0:00 Call to worship
0:47 Hymn 5 A.M.
1:44 The commandments of the grind
2:47 The reading: what hour 70 produced in 1916
4:58 Testimonies, and the day of rest
6:37 The collection
7:06 Revelation: 55 hours a week
8:09 Baptism in cold brew
8:54 Monday, 5 a.m.

The studies:
Pencavel (2014 working paper; Economic Journal, 2015) re-analyzed weekly records collected during the First World War by investigators of Britain's Health of Munition Workers Committee: about a year (1916) of weekly hours and output for four groups of workers, most of them women, in one large factory. Up to about 49 hours a week, output rose in proportion to hours; above that, it rose at a decreasing rate and peaked at about 63 hours. In his estimates, output at 70 hours differed little from output at 56. Holding weekly hours constant, weeks without a day of rest (Sunday) produced about 10% less, and 48 hours over six days (8 a day) produced slightly more (about 1.4%) than 70 hours over seven (10 a day). Limits: factory work in wartime, a century ago, with a small number of observations. It did not measure office work.
Pega et al. (2021), the first joint WHO/ILO estimates: drawing on systematic reviews, people working 55 hours a week or more had about a 35% higher risk of stroke (non-fatal events) and about a 17% higher risk of dying from ischemic heart disease, compared with people working 35 to 40 hours. The evidence comes from observational studies; the authors say they cannot be certain the association is causal.
This video is satire about a work culture. It isn't medical, legal or financial advice.

Pencavel, J. (2015). The productivity of working hours. The Economic Journal, 125(589), 2052-2076. doi:10.1111/ecoj.12166 (IZA Discussion Paper No. 8129, 2014).
Pega, F., Náfrádi, B., Momen, N. C., et al. (2021). Global, regional, and national burdens of ischemic heart disease and stroke attributable to exposure to long working hours for 194 countries, 2000-2016: A systematic analysis from the WHO/ILO Joint Estimates of the Work-related Burden of Disease and Injury. Environment International, 154, 106595. doi:10.1016/j.envint.2021.106595

snippet.title: Maha Mantra in 16 Seconds: Attract Good Karma (or Just Lower Your Cortisol)
snippet.description:
Hare Kṛṣṇa Hare Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇa Hare Hare, Hare Rāma Hare Rāma, Rāma Rāma Hare Hare.

What it is: the Hare Krishna maha mantra ("great mantra"), sixteen Sanskrit words from the Kali-Santarana Upanishad, sung every day in the Gaudiya Vaishnava tradition and carried around the world by ISKCON since 1966. All three words are a call: Hare addresses Harā, the Lord's energy (Rādhā); Kṛṣṇa and Rāma are names of God. Say it HAH-ray, KRISH-nuh, RAH-muh.

In the tradition: Prabhupada explained it as a prayer, "O energy of the Lord, O Lord, please engage me in Your service". The Upanishad's name means "crossing over Kali": these sixteen names are said to carry you through the age of quarrel.

Why a sound like this can calm you: in a 2001 BMJ study, 23 healthy adults recited the rosary and a yoga mantra; both slowed breathing to about 6 breaths a minute and made the heart-rhythm reflexes stronger (Bernardi et al.). In a 2024 study, 34 adults chanted "om" for 12 minutes, aloud or silently, and their saliva cortisol and anxiety went down (Perry, Polito & Thompson); there was no group that didn't chant. In a small 2006 lab study, slow music and pauses lowered heart rate and breathing (Bernardi, Porta & Sleight). Small studies, short effects: calmer, not cured.

And if karma is real, this should clean a little of yours. The tradition says singing the names "cleans the mirror of the heart" and grows joy (Chaitanya's Shikshashtaka, verse 1). Good karma, joy, or both.

Sing it with her once. Then again.

Sources:
Bernardi, L., Sleight, P., Bandinelli, G., et al. (2001). Effect of rosary prayer and yoga mantras on autonomic cardiovascular rhythms: comparative study. BMJ, 323(7327), 1446-1449. doi:10.1136/bmj.323.7327.1446
Perry, G., Polito, V., & Thompson, W. F. (2024). Exploring the physiological and psychological effects of group chanting in Australia: Reduced stress, cortisol and enhanced social connection. Journal of Religion and Health, 63(6), 4793-4815. doi:10.1007/s10943-023-01967-5
Bernardi, L., Porta, C., & Sleight, P. (2006). Cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, and respiratory changes induced by different types of music in musicians and non-musicians: the importance of silence. Heart, 92(4), 445-452. doi:10.1136/hrt.2005.064600
Kali-Santarana Upanishad; Prabhupada on Harā and the vocative (Vanisource); Shikshashtaka 1.

Voice: synthetic (ElevenLabs). Drone, tanpura and bowl composed with code by NAOS. Corrections welcome.

snippet.title: Om Mani Padme Hum x5: Cleanse Your Karma (or Just Lower Your Cortisol)
snippet.description:
Oṃ Maṇi Padme Hūṃ, said the Tibetan way: Om Mani Peme Hung.

What it is: the six-syllable mantra of Avalokiteśvara (Chenrezig in Tibetan), the bodhisattva of compassion, recited, carved and spun in prayer wheels across Tibetan Buddhism. Mani means jewel and padme lotus; the Dalai Lama explains the jewel as compassion and the lotus as wisdom. The Sanskrit is Om Mani Padme Hum; Tibetans say "peme" and "hung", and that's how it's chanted here.

In the tradition: it is chanted to call up Chenrezig's compassion for all beings. The Dalai Lama teaches that the six syllables stand for a path that unites method and wisdom, which can turn an impure body, speech and mind into those of a Buddha.

Why a sound like this can calm you: in a 2001 BMJ study, 23 healthy adults recited "om-mani-padme-om" and the rosary; both slowed breathing to about 6 breaths a minute and made the heart-rhythm reflexes stronger (Bernardi et al.). In a 2024 study, 34 adults chanted "om" for 12 minutes and their saliva cortisol and anxiety went down (Perry, Polito & Thompson); there was no group that didn't chant. In a pilot brain scan of 12 people, chanting "om" lowered activity in emotion areas, the amygdala among them, compared with rest; saying "ssss" did not (Kalyani et al., 2011). Small studies, short effects: calmer, not cured.

And if karma is real, this should clean a little of yours. Good karma, joy, or both.

Chant it five times with him. Then once more.

Sources:
Bernardi, L., Sleight, P., Bandinelli, G., et al. (2001). Effect of rosary prayer and yoga mantras on autonomic cardiovascular rhythms: comparative study. BMJ, 323(7327), 1446-1449. doi:10.1136/bmj.323.7327.1446
Perry, G., Polito, V., & Thompson, W. F. (2024). Exploring the physiological and psychological effects of group chanting in Australia: Reduced stress, cortisol and enhanced social connection. Journal of Religion and Health, 63(6), 4793-4815. doi:10.1007/s10943-023-01967-5
Kalyani, B. G., Venkatasubramanian, G., Arasappa, R., et al. (2011). Neurohemodynamic correlates of 'OM' chanting: A pilot functional magnetic resonance imaging study. International Journal of Yoga, 4(1), 3-6. doi:10.4103/0973-6131.78171
The Dalai Lama, On the meaning of Om Mani Padme Hum (sacred-texts.com/bud/tib/omph.htm).

In the tradition: it is chanted to call up Chenrezig's compassion for all beings. The Dalai Lama teaches that the six syllables stand for a path that unites method and wisdom, which can turn an impure body, speech and mind into those of a Buddha.

Small studies, short effects, a few minutes at a time: calmer, not cured. None of them tested a video like this one, a whole session, studying or karma.

And if karma is real, this should clean a little of yours. Good karma, a calmer week, or both. No promises, no cure.

Ways to use it: sing the first eight rounds with the single voice and let your breath slow down; put it on while you cook or tidy; play it before a hard conversation or at the end of a long day; or keep it low while you work. Listening only is fine too.

snippet.title: Hare Krishna Maha Mantra to Sing Along, 108 Times (21 Min Kirtan That Speeds Up)
snippet.description:
The Hare Krishna maha mantra, 108 times, sung kirtan style in 21 minutes: first one voice, then call and response, then everyone with a band that keeps speeding up, and back down to a whisper. Sing along: the word being sung lights up on screen with its meaning underneath, and a mala of 108 beads fills at the top.

Hare Kṛṣṇa Hare Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇa Hare Hare, Hare Rāma Hare Rāma, Rāma Rāma Hare Hare.

What it is: the Hare Krishna maha mantra ("great mantra"), sixteen Sanskrit words from the Kali-Santarana Upanishad, sung every day in the Gaudiya Vaishnava tradition and carried around the world by ISKCON since 1966. All three words are a call: Hare addresses Harā, the Lord's energy (Rādhā); Kṛṣṇa and Rāma are names of God. Say it HAH-ray, KRISH-nuh, RAH-muh.

In the tradition: Prabhupada explained it as a prayer, "O energy of the Lord, O Lord, please engage me in Your service". The Upanishad's name means "crossing over Kali": these sixteen names are said to carry you through the age of quarrel. Chanting them with others is called kirtan.

Why a repeated sound can calm you: in a 2001 BMJ study, 23 healthy adults recited "om-mani-padme-om" and the rosary; both slowed breathing to about 6 breaths a minute and made the heart-rhythm reflexes stronger (Bernardi et al.). In a 2024 study, 34 adults chanted "om" for 12 minutes and their saliva cortisol and anxiety went down (Perry, Polito & Thompson); there was no group that didn't chant. In a pilot brain scan of 12 people, chanting "om" lowered activity in emotion areas, the amygdala among them, compared with rest; saying "ssss" did not (Kalyani et al., 2011). Small studies, short effects, a few minutes at a time: calmer, not cured. None of them tested a video like this one, a whole session, studying or karma.

And if karma is real, this should clean a little of yours. The tradition says singing the names "cleans the mirror of the heart" and grows joy (Chaitanya's Shikshashtaka, verse 1). Good karma, joy, a calmer week, or all three. No promises, no cure.

Ways to use it: sing the first rounds along with the single voice and let your breath slow down; put it on while you cook or tidy; play it before a hard conversation or at the end of a long day; or keep it low while you work. Listening only is fine too.

Perry, G., Polito, V., & Thompson, W. F. (2024). Exploring the physiological and psychological effects of group chanting in Australia: Reduced stress, cortisol and enhanced social connection. Journal of Religion and Health, 63(6), 4793-4815. doi:10.1007/s10943-023-01967-5
Kalyani, B. G., Venkatasubramanian, G., Arasappa, R., et al. (2011). Neurohemodynamic correlates of 'OM' chanting: A pilot functional magnetic resonance imaging study. International Journal of Yoga, 4(1), 3-6. doi:10.4103/0973-6131.78171
